name: Livestock Nutrition and Feed Formulation with Local Ingredients
objectives: Given a class of animal and its stage, list the nutrients it needs (energy, protein, minerals and water) and a local feed that supplies each one, naming one correct feed for each nutrient
Given the feeds available near you, sort local ingredients and fodder into energy feeds, protein feeds, roughage and supplements, with at least 8 of 10 placed correctly

Given two ingredients and a target protein level, balance a ration with the Pearson square and write the kg of each ingredient per 100 kg of mix, with the mix within 0.5 percentage points of the target
Using fodder and feed on your farm, make silage or hay and store feed so it stays dry and free of mould, following every step of the checklist
For one class of animal, write a staged feeding plan with basal feed or forage, concentrate and supplements for each stage, covering every stage from young to market, lay or milk
Using your local prices and records, calculate the feed cost per kg of mix and per kg of gain, tray of eggs or litre of milk, with correct arithmetic and every ingredient included

chapters.name: Chapter 1: What animals need and what you have

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Nutrients: energy, protein, minerals and water
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List what an animal needs to eat and drink, and a local feed for each need.
This lesson builds toward: Given a class of animal and its stage, you will list the nutrients it needs (energy, protein, minerals and water) and a local feed that supplies each one, naming one correct feed for each nutrient.
Every animal needs four things from its feed and water. Energy keeps it alive, warm and moving, and fuels growth, milk and eggs; it comes mainly from grains (maize, sorghum, cassava), brans and fresh or conserved grass. Protein builds muscle, milk, eggs and young; it comes from oilseed cakes (soybean, cotton seed, groundnut, sunflower), fish meal and legumes such as desmodium and lablab. Minerals and vitamins build bones and eggshells and keep the body working: salt, calcium from limestone or shells, phosphorus and a mineral and vitamin premix.
Water is the most important nutrient and the cheapest. An animal goes off feed fast without it, and milking cows and laying hens drink a lot. Give clean water all the time, more in hot weather, in clean drinkers in the shade.
Needs change with the animal and its stage. A young, fast-growing animal, a laying hen and a milking cow need more protein than an adult at rest. Cattle, goats and sheep are ruminants: their stomach can digest grass and crop residues, so roughage is the base of their diet. Pigs and poultry cannot digest much roughage, so they need grain-based mashes with protein, minerals and vitamins mixed in.
Words to know:
- Nutrient: a part of feed the body needs: energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and water.
- Ruminant: an animal with a four-part stomach that can digest grass: cattle, goats and sheep.
- Premix: a bought mix of minerals and vitamins added in small amounts to feed, as the label says.
- Roughage: bulky, fibre-rich feed such as grass, hay, silage and crop residues.
Official sources:
- Feedipedia (INRAE, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO): animal feed resources information system
Try it now: Pick one class of animal on your farm (for example growing pigs, layers or a milking cow). Write its four needs and, next to each, one feed you can get locally that supplies it.
You can now list the energy, protein, mineral and water needs of an animal and name a local feed for each.

check.q: Which nutrient is the cheapest and the most important?
check.why: Animals quickly stop eating and producing without clean water.
Oilseed cakes such as soybean cake are rich in protein; maize and cassava mainly give energy.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Local ingredients and fodder
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Sort the feeds you can get into energy feeds, protein feeds, roughage and supplements.
This lesson builds toward: Given the feeds available near you, you will sort local ingredients and fodder into energy feeds, protein feeds, roughage and supplements, with at least 8 of 10 placed correctly.
Energy feeds: maize, sorghum and millet grain, cassava (peeled, dried or processed so it is safe), maize bran and wheat bran. Brans are cheaper than grain and give some protein and fibre, but too much bran in a poultry mash dilutes the energy. Maize grain has only about 8 to 10 percent protein, so on its own it cannot feed a growing animal.
Protein feeds: soybean cake (often around 44 to 48 percent protein, depending on how it was made), cotton seed cake, groundnut cake, sunflower cake and fish meal (such as omena in Kenya). Cotton seed cake contains gossypol, which can harm pigs, poultry and young animals, so use it only within the limits in a feed guide or from a nutritionist. Fish meal is rich but costly and its quality varies: buy from a trusted source and check that it is not mixed with sand or salt.
Fodder and roughage for ruminants: Napier grass, Brachiaria grass, maize stover, legumes such as desmodium and lablab, and tree leaves such as leucaena and calliandra. Legumes are high in protein and can replace part of the bought concentrate. icipe's push-pull system grows desmodium between maize rows and Napier or Brachiaria around the field: it protects the maize from pests and gives high-quality fodder. Supplements: salt, limestone or shells for calcium, and a mineral and vitamin premix used as the label says.
Step by step:
- List every feed you can buy or grow within easy reach.
- Mark each one: energy, protein, roughage or supplement.
- Write its price per kg and when in the year you can get it.
- Ask your supplier or extension officer for its protein value.
- Note any limits, such as cotton seed cake for pigs and poultry.
Words to know:
- Concentrate: feed rich in energy or protein, such as grain, bran, oilseed cake or a bought dairy meal.
- Oilseed cake: what is left after oil is pressed from seeds such as soybean or cotton seed; rich in protein.
- Legume: a plant such as desmodium, lablab or beans that is rich in protein and adds nitrogen to soil.
- Gossypol: a natural substance in cotton seed that can harm pigs, poultry and young animals.
Official sources:
- Feedipedia: Maize grain (protein about 8 to 10.5 percent of dry matter)
- Feedipedia: Soybean meal (protein by type)
- icipe: Push-pull technology (desmodium, Napier and Brachiaria as fodder)
Try it now: Make a table of 8 to 10 feeds you can get near you with four columns: feed, type (energy, protein, roughage or supplement), price per kg, and months available.
You can now sort the feeds near you into energy feeds, protein feeds, roughage and supplements, and note their prices and limits.

check.q: Which is a protein-rich fodder legume for cattle and goats?
check.why: Desmodium is a legume, rich in protein; the others mainly give energy or fibre.

check.q: Why should you be careful with cotton seed cake for pigs and poultry?
options: It contains gossypol, which can harm them
check.why: Gossypol in cotton seed can harm pigs, poultry and young animals, so use it within guide limits.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Balancing a ration with the Pearson square
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Balance two ingredients to a target protein level with the Pearson square.
This lesson builds toward: Given two ingredients and a target protein level, you will balance a ration with the Pearson square and write the kg of each ingredient per 100 kg of mix, with the mix within 0.5 percentage points of the target.
The Pearson square is a simple drawing that tells you how much of two feeds to mix to hit one target, usually protein. It works with one nutrient and two feeds at a time, and the target must be between the two feeds' values. Use values on the same basis (both as-fed or both dry matter).
Worked example with typical values (check yours): maize at 9 percent protein, soybean cake at 44 percent, and a target of 18 percent. Your target comes from a feed guide, your extension officer or a nutritionist for that animal and stage. Draw a square. Write 18 in the middle, maize 9 at the top left and soybean cake 44 at the bottom left. Subtract across the diagonals and ignore minus signs: 44 minus 18 = 26 parts of maize (top right); 18 minus 9 = 9 parts of soybean cake (bottom right). Total parts = 26 + 9 = 35.
Turn parts into kg per 100 kg: maize = 26 / 35 x 100 = 74.3 kg; soybean cake = 9 / 35 x 100 = 25.7 kg. Check: 74.3 x 9 % = 6.7 kg protein, plus 25.7 x 44 % = 11.3 kg, total 18.0 kg of protein in 100 kg: 18 percent. In a real mash you first set aside space for fixed items (premix, salt, limestone for layers, as the label or guide says), then use the square for the rest. The square balances protein only, so check energy, fibre and minerals with your extension officer.
Step by step:
- Write the target protein in the middle of a square.
- Write feed A (low protein) top left and feed B (high protein) bottom left.
- Subtract across each diagonal; ignore minus signs.
- Top right = parts of feed A; bottom right = parts of feed B.
- Divide each by the total parts and multiply by 100 for kg per 100 kg.
- Check: kg x protein percent for each feed adds up to the target.
Words to know:
- Pearson square: a simple drawing that shows how much of two feeds to mix to hit one nutrient target.
- Crude protein: the protein value printed on feed labels and lab reports, as a percent.
- Ration: the feed an animal gets in a day, or the mix it is fed from.
- As-fed: measured as the feed is, with its water in; dry matter values remove the water.
Official sources:
- University of Tennessee Extension: Feedstuffs activity packet (the Pearson square)
- Feedipedia: Maize grain (protein about 8 to 10.5 percent of dry matter)
- Feedipedia: Soybean meal (protein by type)
Try it now: Use the Pearson square to mix maize bran (use 10 percent protein as a practice value) with soybean cake (44 percent) for a 16 percent target. Write kg per 100 kg and check the protein adds up. (Answer: 28 parts bran and 6 parts cake, so 82.4 kg and 17.6 kg.)
You can now balance two feeds to a protein target with the Pearson square and check the result.

check.q: In the Pearson square, what goes in the middle?
check.why: The target nutrient level goes in the middle; the feeds go on the left.

check.q: You mix maize (9 percent) and soybean cake (44 percent) for 18 percent. How many parts of maize?
check.why: Subtract across the diagonal: 44 - 18 = 26 parts of maize.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Conserve, plan and cost your feed

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Silage, hay and safe feed storage
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make silage or hay and store feed so it stays dry and free of mould.
This lesson builds toward: Using fodder and feed on your farm, you will make silage or hay and store feed so it stays dry and free of mould, following every step of the checklist.
In the rainy season there is too much grass; in the dry season too little, and milk and weight drop. Conserving fodder evens this out. Silage is green fodder (maize, sorghum or Napier) kept without air so it ferments and stays moist and good to eat for months. Hay is grass or legume cut and dried in the sun until it is dry enough to store without rotting.
Silage, the FAO way: chop small, fill quickly, compact hard and seal airtight. Cut maize or sorghum when the grain is soft and milky to doughy. Chop the fodder into short pieces, fill the pit, plastic tube, bag or clean drum fast, press out every pocket of air by trampling or packing, then seal with plastic and weigh it down. Napier and other grasses are low in sugar; farmers often add molasses to help them ferment (ask your extension officer how much). Leave it closed for some weeks, and once opened, take out what you need each day and close it again. Good silage smells sweet-sour; throw away mouldy or rotten parts.
Moulds on feed can make mycotoxins, such as aflatoxin. They are invisible poisons that cut growth, milk and fertility, make animals sick, and can pass into milk, eggs and meat. ILRI studies in Kenya found aflatoxin in many dairy feeds. Prevent it: buy feed from trusted mills, check it is dry, free-flowing and smells fresh, store bags on pallets off the floor and away from walls, under a roof that does not leak, use the oldest feed first, and never feed mouldy feed, even to other animals.
Step by step:
- Silage: harvest at the right stage and chop small.
- Fill the pit, tube, bag or drum quickly and compact hard to push out air.
- Seal airtight with plastic and weigh it down; leave it closed for some weeks.
- Hay: cut, dry in the sun, turn often, store dry under a roof.
- Feed store: pallets off the floor, away from walls, roof that does not leak.
- Use oldest feed first; throw away anything mouldy, caked or smelling bad.
Words to know:
- Silage: green fodder kept airtight so it ferments and stays good to feed for months.
- Hay: grass or legume cut and dried in the sun for storage.
- Mycotoxin: a poison made by moulds on feed, such as aflatoxin; it cannot be seen.
- Pallet: a raised wooden or plastic platform that keeps bags off the floor.
Official sources:
- FAO: Harvesting and ensiling techniques (silage making in the tropics)
- FAO: Silage making for small-scale farmers (conclusions: bag silage, low-cost methods)
- ILRI: Mycotoxin binders, an option for safer milk in Kenya?
Try it now: Walk to where you store feed. Write three things that could let in damp or mould, and how you will fix each. Then plan one batch of silage or hay: what fodder, when to cut it, and what you will store it in.
You can now make silage or hay and store feed in a way that keeps out damp, mould and mycotoxins.

check.q: What is the most important thing when making silage?
options: Leaving it open so it can breathe
Pushing out the air and sealing it airtight
check.why: Silage keeps only when air is pushed out and kept out, so it can ferment.

check.q: A bag of dairy meal has grey, caked lumps and smells musty. What do you do?
options: Feed it to the dry cows
Feed it to the chickens instead
Do not feed it to any animal
check.why: Mould can carry mycotoxins that harm every animal and can pass into milk and eggs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Feeding by stage: a three-part feed plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a feed plan for each stage of one class of animal.
This lesson builds toward: For one class of animal, you will write a staged feeding plan with basal feed or forage, concentrate and supplements for each stage, covering every stage from young to market, lay or milk.
Animals need different feeds at different stages. Broilers: starter, then finisher (some farmers add a grower in between). Layers: chick mash, then growers mash, then layers mash from the point of lay, with extra calcium for the eggshells. Pigs: creep or weaner feed, grower, finisher, then special feeds for pregnant and suckling sows. Dairy cattle: calf, heifer, dry cow and lactation, with the concentrate matched to the milk each cow gives. Change from one feed to the next over a few days, not overnight.
Use a simple three-part plan for each stage. Part 1, the basal feed: what most of the diet is made of. For cattle and goats this is forage (grazing, Napier, hay, silage, stover); for pigs and poultry it is the energy grains and brans in the mash. Part 2, the concentrate: the protein-rich part (oilseed cakes, fish meal, a bought dairy meal or a balanced mash) that tops up what the basal feed lacks. Part 3, supplements: salt, minerals, vitamins and calcium, used as the label says. Plus clean water all the time.
Feeding to stage saves money: you do not pay for high-protein starter feed for an animal that no longer needs it. Weigh or estimate how much each stage eats and watch the animals: if they are thin, lay less or milk less, ask your extension officer to check the plan. The bag label or hatchery or breed guide says when to change feeds for commercial breeds.
Step by step:
- Choose one class of animal.
- List its stages from young to market, lay or milk.
- For each stage write the basal feed.
- Add the concentrate that tops it up.
- Add supplements and water.
- Write when to change to the next stage, and change over a few days.
Words to know:
- Basal feed: the main part of the diet: forage for ruminants, energy grains for pigs and poultry.
- Point of lay: the age when young hens are about to start laying eggs.
- Lactation: the time a female is producing milk.
Official sources:
- Feedipedia (INRAE, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO): animal feed resources information system
Try it now: Choose one class of animal. Write a table with one row per stage and four columns: basal feed, concentrate, supplements, and when to change to the next stage.
You can now write a staged feeding plan with basal feed, concentrate and supplements for each stage.

check.q: In a three-part feed plan for a dairy cow, what is the basal feed?
options: Forage such as Napier grass, hay or silage
check.why: For ruminants, forage makes up most of the diet; concentrate and supplements top it up.

check.q: Your pullets are close to the point of lay. Which feed do they move to?
options: Layers mash, changed over a few days
check.why: Layers mash gives the extra calcium needed for eggshells; change slowly over a few days.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Costing your feed per kg of gain or litre of milk
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost of your ration per kg, and the feed cost per kg of gain, tray of eggs or litre of milk.
This lesson builds toward: Using your local prices and records, you will calculate the feed cost per kg of mix and per kg of gain, tray of eggs or litre of milk, with correct arithmetic and every ingredient included.
Step 1, cost per kg of mix. Multiply the kg of each ingredient by its price, add them up and divide by the total kg. Example with made-up Kenya shilling prices: 74.3 kg maize at KES 40 = 2,972; 25.7 kg soybean cake at KES 90 = 2,313. Total KES 5,285 for 100 kg, so KES 52.85 per kg. Add milling, transport and premix if you pay for them.
Step 2, feed per unit of product. For meat, record the feed eaten and the weight gained: if 10 pigs eat 900 kg of grower feed and gain 300 kg, each kg of gain took 3 kg of feed (the feed conversion ratio, FCR). Feed cost per kg of gain = 3 x KES 52.85 = KES 158.55. For eggs: feed eaten by the flock in a week x price per kg, divided by trays collected. For milk: the cow's daily feed cost (forage plus dairy meal) divided by the litres she gives that day.
Use the numbers to decide. Compare the feed cost per kg of gain or per litre with your selling price. Try a cheaper ingredient, such as more fodder legumes or local bran, but check it still meets the target and does not cut growth or milk. Work in your own currency, whether NGN, GHS or XOF: the method is the same. Prices change, so update the sheet every time you buy.
Step by step:
- List each ingredient, its kg per 100 kg and its price per kg.
- Multiply kg by price for each ingredient and add them up.
- Add milling, transport and premix costs; divide by the total kg.
- Record feed eaten and weight gained, eggs or milk produced.
- Feed cost per kg of gain = FCR x cost per kg of feed.
- Feed cost per litre or tray = feed cost for the day or week / litres or trays.
Words to know:
- Feed conversion ratio (FCR): kg of feed needed for 1 kg of weight gain; lower is better.
- Cost per kg of gain: the feed money spent for each kg the animal grows.
- Tray: a tray of 30 eggs, the usual unit for selling eggs.
Try it now: Final task: make a costed ration for one class of animal. Write the three-part plan, balance the concentrate with the Pearson square, list kg per 100 kg, cost it per kg with your local prices, and work out the feed cost per kg of gain, per tray of eggs or per litre of milk.
You can now cost a ration per kg and work out your feed cost per kg of gain, tray of eggs or litre of milk.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Class, stage and three-part plan No class or stage named, or one of basal feed, concentrate and supplements is missing. Names the class and stage and gives the basal feed, concentrate, supplements and water. Also shows the next stage and when and how to change feed. Ingredients sorted and suitable Ingredients are wrongly sorted or unsafe (for example mouldy, or cotton seed cake with no limit for poultry). Uses local ingredients correctly sorted into energy, protein, roughage and supplements. Uses a cheaper local legume or bran and explains how it keeps the target. Pearson square No working shown, or the target is not between the two feeds. Square drawn, parts and kg per 100 kg correct, and the check adds up to the target within 0.5 points. Sets aside fixed items such as premix first and balances the rest. Costing Cost per kg is missing or the arithmetic is wrong. Correct cost per kg of mix and feed cost per kg of gain, tray of eggs or litre of milk, in local currency. Compares it with the selling price and shows one way to cut the cost. Feed quality and storage Says nothing about where feed is kept or how mould is avoided. States where feed is stored and how it is kept dry and mould-free, oldest first. Includes a silage or hay plan for the dry season. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the ration and check it again.

check.q: 100 kg of mix costs XOF 20,000 in total. What is the cost per kg?
Broilers ate 400 kg of feed and gained 250 kg. What is the FCR?
